claims.claim: SecE reinforces the SecY conformation on one side.
claims.source: This conformation is reinforced on one side by SecE, while on the opposite side a lateral gate (LG) connects the central protein-conducting channel to the lipid bilayer (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on structural data.

claims.claim: A lateral gate (LG) connects the central protein-conducting channel to the lipid bilayer.
claims.source: This conformation is reinforced on one side by SecE, while on the opposite side a lateral gate (LG) connects the central protein-conducting channel to the lipid bilayer (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on structural data.

claims.claim: Opening of the 'clamshell' could facilitate passage of secretory proteins through the central channel across the membrane.
claims.source: Thus, opening of the 'clamshell' could facilitate passage of secretory proteins through the central channel across the membrane, as well as the partitioning of membrane proteins via the LG into the bilayer.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of the clamshell opening.

claims.claim: Opening of the 'clamshell' could facilitate the partitioning of membrane proteins via the LG into the bilayer.
claims.source: Thus, opening of the 'clamshell' could facilitate passage of secretory proteins through the central channel across the membrane, as well as the partitioning of membrane proteins via the LG into the bilayer.

claims.claim: SecA is a cytoplasmic ATPase that drives protein translocation through SecYEG.
claims.source: SecA is a cytoplasmic ATPase that drives protein translocation through SecYEG (Lill et al., 1989; Brundage et al., 1990; Akimaru et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The ATP turnover cycle of SecA is directly coupled to protein translocation.
claims.source: The ATP turnover cycle of SecA is directly coupled to protein translocation (Economou and Wickner, 1994; Karamanou et al., 1999), but as yet the mechanism by which this is accomplished is unclear.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which ATP turnover is coupled to protein translocation is unclear.

claims.claim: SecA consists of two RecA-like nucleotide binding domains (NBD1 and NBD2), which together form the nucleotide-binding site (NBS).
claims.source: Structural studies have revealed that SecA consists of two RecA-like nucleotide binding domains (NBD1 and NBD2), which together form the nucleotide-binding site (NBS) (Hunt et al., 2002) (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous structural studies and reference to Figure 1B.

claims.claim: A 'two-helix finger' (2HF) is at the SecY binding interface.
claims.source: A 'two-helix finger' (2HF), at the SecY binding interface (Zimmer et al., 2008), and a pre-protein cross-linking domain (PPXD) both make contacts with the translocating polypeptide (Bauer and Rapoport, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The 2HF and PPXD both make contacts with the translocating polypeptide.

claims.claim: SecY and SecA interact tightly, with the 2HF from SecA protruding into the SecY channel.
claims.source: SecY and SecA interact tightly, with the 2HF from SecA protruding into the SecY channel, and a long loop between TMs 6–7 of SecY buried inside SecA (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: A long loop between TMs 6–7 of SecY is buried inside SecA.

claims.claim: A large movement of the PPXD activates the ATPase.
claims.source: In SecA, a large movement of the PPXD activates the ATPase (Gold et al., 2013) and is thought to clamp the substrate in place, while in SecYEG the LG opens, causing a widening of the channel through which translocating substrates pass (Figure 1B) (Zimmer et al., 2008).

claims.claim: The PPXD movement is thought to clamp the substrate in place.

claims.claim: In SecYEG the LG opens, causing a widening of the channel through which translocating substrates pass.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and reference to Figure 1B.

claims.claim: When ADP-BeFx was replaced with ATP, the LG either retained its part-open ('PO') state of about 1.8 nm or widened further to ~2.6 nm forming an open state ('O').
claims.source: When ADP-BeFx was replaced with ATP, the LG either retained its part-open ('PO') state of about 1.8 nm (Figure 2A, middle panel, compare to Figure 2B, lower panel; Figure 2C) or widened further to ~2.6 nm forming an open state ('O'; Figure 2A, lower panel; Figure 2C).

claims.claim: Substitution of ADP-BeFx with ADP resulted in LG closure in all five simulations to ~1.5 nm ('C').

claims.claim: The closed state closely resembles a previous structure of the resting SecY-complex in the absence of SecA (1RHZ).
claims.source: Remarkably, this closed state closely resembles a previous structure of the resting SecY-complex in the absence of SecA (1RHZ (Van den Berg et al., 2004); Figure 2B, upper panel and Figure 2C).

claims.claim: Simulations using a different molecular mechanics force field (Amber ff99SB-ILDN) show a similar effect.

claims.claim: The configuration of helicase motif residues correlates to the open or closed state of the channel.
claims.source: In this system the configuration of these residues correlates to the open or closed state of the channel (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: All the ADP and ATP trajectories diverge within the first 10 ns.
claims.source: Nonetheless, the initial opening or closing event is rapid: all the ADP and ATP trajectories diverge within the first 10 ns (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The speed of divergence suggests that the input model represents a high-energy intermediate – probably due to the presence of ADP-BeFx.

claims.claim: Donor (Alexa Fluor 488) and acceptor (Alexa Fluor 594) fluorescent probes were attached to a unique cysteine pair flanking the LG (A103 and V353 of Escherichia coli SecY).
claims.source: To test the MD results experimentally, donor (Alexa Fluor 488) and acceptor (Alexa Fluor 594) fluorescent probes were attached to a unique cysteine pair flanking the LG (A103 and V353 of Escherichia coli SecY; Figure 4A; Cβ-Cβ distances 3.4–4.4 nm; the Förster radius, R0, is 6 nm for the chosen dye pair).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for FRET measurements.

claims.claim: The doubly labelled protein (SecY**EG) is active.
claims.source: The doubly labelled protein (hereafter SecY**EG) is active (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and limited proteolysis confirms equal labelling on both sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B+C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Limited proteolysis confirms equal labelling on both sites of SecY**EG.
claims.source: The doubly labelled protein (hereafter SecY**EG) is active (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and limited proteolysis confirms equal labelling on both sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B+C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B+C.

claims.claim: About 50% of the complexes face outwards after reconstitution into proteo-liposomes (PLs).
claims.source: After reconstitution into proteo-liposomes (PLs), about 50% (as judged by trypsin protection) of the complexes face outwards (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), as has been observed previously for wild-type SecYEG (Mao et al., 2013; Schulze et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Equilibrium fluorescence measurements of SecY**EG show a decrease in FRET upon binding of SecA.
claims.source: Equilibrium fluorescence measurements of SecY**EG show a decrease in FRET upon binding of SecA (Figure 4B), indicating LG movement – as expected from the crystal structures.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: A further FRET decrease is observed upon addition of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue AMPPNP, but not ADP.
claims.source: A further FRET decrease is observed upon addition of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue AMPPNP, but not ADP (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The changes in apparent FRET efficiency are not caused by differences in affinity between SecYEG and SecA in different nucleotide states, but rather represent differences in the width of the LG.
claims.source: Titration of SecA into SecY**EG PLs in the presence of either ADP or AMPPNP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) shows that the changes in apparent FRET efficiency are not caused by differences in affinity between SecYEG and SecA in different nucleotide states, but rather represent differences in the width of the LG, i.e. a closure of the LG in the presence of ADP on SecA, some 5 nm away – consistent with the MD results.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and is consistent with MD simulation results.

claims.claim: PLs containing single copies of SecY**EG were tethered to a glass supported bilayer.
claims.source: PLs containing single copies of SecY**EG were tethered to a glass supported bilayer as previously described (Figure 5A) (Deville et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for single molecule FRET measurements.

claims.claim: Particles containing a single FRET pair as judged by sequential single step photobleaching of both dyes were selected for FRET analysis.
claims.source: From time-lapse TIRF images, particles containing a single FRET pair as judged by sequential single step photobleaching of both dyes were selected for FRET analysis (see Materials and methods and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for details).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for single molecule FRET measurements.

claims.claim: In the absence of SecA or nucleotide, SecY**EG exists mainly as a single population with an average FRET efficiency (EFRET) of 0.76.
claims.source: In the absence of SecA or nucleotide, SecY**EG exists mainly as a single population with an average FRET efficiency (EFRET) of 0.76 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Addition of SecA causes the open states to become more populated, with the relative populations dependent on which nucleotide is provided.
claims.source: In accord with the ensemble data, addition of SecA causes the open states to become more populated, with the relative populations dependent on which nucleotide is provided (Figure 5C–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–G.

claims.claim: At least three components are required to fully describe the histogram distribution with ATP.
claims.source: While a two state model could fit the majority of the distributions (data not shown) both global non-linear fitting (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A) and singular value decomposition (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B) indicate that at least three components are required to fully describe the histogram distribution with ATP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Three principal states were used to fit the entire dataset: (1) closed, EFRET ~0.76; (2) part-open, EFRET ~0.59; and (3) open, EFRET ~0.45.
claims.source: Therefore three principal states were used to fit the entire dataset: (1) closed, EFRET ~0.76 (red); (2) part-open, EFRET ~0.59 (green); and (3) open, EFRET ~0.45 (blue).
claims.evidence: This describes the data analysis approach for the single molecule FRET experiments.

claims.claim: The difference between the open and closed state is ~0.9 nm.
claims.source: Assuming an R0 of 6 nm, the difference between the open and closed state is ~0.9 nm – consistent with the changes observed across LG by MD (Figure 2C) and those expected from the crystal structures (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of FRET data and is consistent with MD simulations and crystal structures.

claims.claim: In the presence of AMPPNP, the LG occupies mainly the open conformation.
claims.source: These data (Figure 5H) show that in the presence of AMPPNP – which traps the complex in an ATP bound-like state—the LG occupies mainly the open conformation (Figure 5C+H), while with ADP the closed state is more highly populated (Figure 5D+H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, 5H.

claims.claim: With ADP the closed state is more highly populated.
claims.source: These data (Figure 5H) show that in the presence of AMPPNP – which traps the complex in an ATP bound-like state—the LG occupies mainly the open conformation (Figure 5C+H), while with ADP the closed state is more highly populated (Figure 5D+H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, 5H.

claims.claim: In the presence of ATP, SecY predominantly populates the part-open state.
claims.source: Intriguingly, in the presence of ATP—which under steady-state conditions is rapidly hydrolysed to ADP (Robson et al., 2009)—SecY predominantly populates the part-open state (Figure 5E+H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E, 5H.

claims.claim: Mathematical modelling indicates that the third state cannot be explained by averaging of the two different nucleotide bound forms during data collection.
claims.source: Mathematical modelling indicates that the third state cannot be explained by averaging of the two different nucleotide bound forms during data collection (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C+D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modelling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C+D.

claims.claim: The part-open state most likely represents a true intermediate on the pathway between the closed and open conformations.
claims.source: So, the part-open state most likely represents a true intermediate on the pathway between the closed and open conformations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical modelling and experimental data.

claims.claim: Addition of pOA + ATP to SecY**EG-SecA causes the open state to dominate.
claims.source: Addition of pOA + ATP to SecY**EG-SecA causes the open state to dominate (Figure 5F+H); an effect consolidated by addition of a large excess of SecA and pOA (Figure 5G+H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F, 5G, 5H.

claims.claim: ADP release is strongly accelerated by the presence of pre-protein, such that the open (ATP-bound) state becomes more highly populated.
claims.source: This is consistent with the known properties of the steady-state cycle of SecA: ADP release is strongly accelerated by the presence of pre-protein, such that the open (ATP-bound) state becomes more highly populated (Robson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: No further states of the channel are detected in the presence of the pre-protein.
claims.source: No further states of the channel are detected in the presence of the pre-protein (Figure 5F+G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F, 5G.

claims.claim: Nucleotide occupancy in SecA regulates the opening of the SecY protein-channel and LG.
claims.source: Taken together, the MD and FRET results show that nucleotide occupancy in SecA regulates the opening of the SecY protein-channel and LG.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined MD and FRET data.

claims.claim: The MD simulations showed differences in the NBS of SecA, which is more open in the ATP simulations compared to those done with ADP bound.
claims.source: In addition to the LG movement, the MD simulations showed differences in the NBS of SecA, which turns out to be more open in the ATP simulations compared to those done with ADP bound (Figure 6A+B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 6A+B.

claims.claim: An open NBS would increase the rate of nucleotide exchange, altering its affinity and turnover.
claims.source: It seems likely that an open NBS would increase the rate of nucleotide exchange, altering its affinity and turnover.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the MD simulation results.

claims.claim: Trapping the LG in a closed position causes a 5-fold reduction in affinity of SecA for AMPPNP.
claims.source: Trapping the LG in a closed position causes a 5-fold reduction in affinity of SecA for AMPPNP (Figure 6C, left), demonstrating that the conformational state of the LG is transmitted to the NBS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The conformational state of the LG is transmitted to the NBS.
claims.source: Trapping the LG in a closed position causes a 5-fold reduction in affinity of SecA for AMPPNP (Figure 6C, left), demonstrating that the conformational state of the LG is transmitted to the NBS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The koff for ADP is slowed by ~50% with a cross-linked LG.
claims.source: We found that the koff is slowed by ~50% with a cross-linked LG (Figure 6D), consistent with the results presented above showing that NBS and LG closure are coordinated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: There is a two-way communication between SecYEG and SecA over a distance of >5 nm: SecA ATP binding and hydrolysis regulate the aperture of the channel, while LG opening and closing controls the ATP affinity and rate of ADP release from SecA.
claims.source: Together, the results establish the existence of a two-way communication between SecYEG and SecA over a distance of >5 nm: SecA ATP binding and hydrolysis regulate the aperture of the channel, while LG opening and closing controls the ATP affinity and rate of ADP release from SecA.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claims.claim: Binding of signal sequence into the LG is known to be an allosteric activator of SecA.
claims.source: Interestingly, binding of signal sequence into the LG is known to be an allosteric activator of SecA (Gouridis et al., 2009; Hizlan et al., 2012): the increase in the turnover of ATP caused by LG opening could provide a basis for this effect.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The increase in the turnover of ATP caused by LG opening could provide a basis for the allosteric activation of SecA by signal sequence binding.
claims.source: Interestingly, binding of signal sequence into the LG is known to be an allosteric activator of SecA (Gouridis et al., 2009; Hizlan et al., 2012): the increase in the turnover of ATP caused by LG opening could provide a basis for this effect.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The 2HF of SecA is situated directly on the path of pre-proteins as they enter the SecY-channel.
claims.source: The 2HF of SecA is situated directly on the path of pre-proteins as they enter the SecY-channel (Figures 1B and 7A+B), and we have previously shown that perturbing the 2HF by cross-linking to SecY (A795C of SecA cross-linked to K268C of SecY; hereafter SecYxEG-SecA2HF; yellow dotted line in Figure 7B) stimulates the ATPase activity of SecA ~25-fold in PLs (Whitehouse et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on structural data shown in Figures 1B and 7A+B.

claims.claim: Perturbing the 2HF by cross-linking to SecY stimulates the ATPase activity of SecA ~25-fold in PLs.
claims.source: The 2HF of SecA is situated directly on the path of pre-proteins as they enter the SecY-channel (Figures 1B and 7A+B), and we have previously shown that perturbing the 2HF by cross-linking to SecY (A795C of SecA cross-linked to K268C of SecY; hereafter SecYxEG-SecA2HF; yellow dotted line in Figure 7B) stimulates the ATPase activity of SecA ~25-fold in PLs (Whitehouse et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The 2HF might be the sensor that couples the movements of the LG and the NBS.
claims.source: At the time, this observation was surprising; however, in light of the results above, we hypothesised that the 2HF might be the sensor that couples the movements of the LG and the NBS.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental results.

claims.claim: The 2HF is known to play a crucial role in coupling ATP hydrolysis to translocation.
claims.source: Indeed, the 2HF is known to play a crucial role in coupling ATP hydrolysis to translocation (Erlandson et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Covalently cross-linked peptides elicit a significant increase in ADP koff.
claims.source: While the cysteine cross-linking site of SecA itself has no effect on the SecYEG stimulated release of ADP (Figure 7D, compare 'wt + SecYEG ' to 'G793C + SecYEG'), covalently cross-linked peptides elicit a significant increase in ADP koff (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The bulkier peptide, AWCWA, has a greater effect than peptides with smaller residues (AGCGA or AFCFA).
claims.source: The bulkier peptide, AWCWA, has a greater effect than peptides with smaller residues (AGCGA or AFCFA).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data for different peptides.

claims.claim: Peptides are sensed at the SecY channel entrance, and this information is transmitted back to the NBS.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that peptides are sensed at the SecY channel entrance, and that this information is transmitted back to the NBS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Both pulling the 2HF away from the channel (with a disulphide bond) and pushing it away (with a bulky peptide) elicit an increase in ADP release.
claims.source: As both pulling the 2HF away from the channel (with a disulphide bond) and pushing it away (with a bulky peptide; Figure 7B) elicit an increase in ADP release, it seems plausible that the 2HF is sensing the passing peptide sterically; the dramatic effects of point mutations in the 2HF (Erlandson et al., 2008; Bauer et al., 2014) are consistent with this interpretation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and is consistent with previous research.

claims.claim: The 2HF is sensing the passing peptide sterically.
claims.source: As both pulling the 2HF away from the channel (with a disulphide bond) and pushing it away (with a bulky peptide; Figure 7B) elicit an increase in ADP release, it seems plausible that the 2HF is sensing the passing peptide sterically; the dramatic effects of point mutations in the 2HF (Erlandson et al., 2008; Bauer et al., 2014) are consistent with this interpretation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the experimental data and is consistent with previous research.

claims.claim: The ease with which a stretch of polypeptide chain passes through the substrate channel depends on the nature of the amino acids in that stretch.
claims.source: Previous studies of translocation by SecYEG-SecA have shown that the ease with which a stretch of polypeptide chain passes through the substrate channel depends on the nature of the amino acids in that stretch (Sato et al., 1997; Bauer et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Poly-glycine regions diffuse freely and rapidly backwards and forth.
claims.source: For example, poly-glycine regions diffuse freely and rapidly backwards and forth (Bauer et al., 2014), while charged amino acids, especially positively charged, are excluded (Nouwen et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Charged amino acids, especially positively charged, are excluded from the channel.
claims.source: For example, poly-glycine regions diffuse freely and rapidly backwards and forth (Bauer et al., 2014), while charged amino acids, especially positively charged, are excluded (Nouwen et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Some combinations of amino acids form secondary structural elements even before they exit the ribosome.
claims.source: It has also been shown that some combinations of amino acids form secondary structural elements even before they exit the ribosome (Hardesty and Kramer, 2001; Lu and Deutsch, 2005), while others remain natively unfolded.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The aperture of the SecY channel is nucleotide-dependent.
claims.source: Given that the aperture of the SecY channel is nucleotide-dependent, we thought it might form a choke point for diffusion of bulky or structured regions of a substrate sequence: in the ADP-bound state, only uncharged, unfolded stretches of polypeptide may pass; whereas the ATP-bound state is less restrictive (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MD and FRET data.

claims.claim: In the ADP-bound state, only uncharged, unfolded stretches of polypeptide may pass; whereas the ATP-bound state is less restrictive.
claims.source: Given that the aperture of the SecY channel is nucleotide-dependent, we thought it might form a choke point for diffusion of bulky or structured regions of a substrate sequence: in the ADP-bound state, only uncharged, unfolded stretches of polypeptide may pass; whereas the ATP-bound state is less restrictive (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental results.

claims.claim: All three substrates (AGAGA, AFAFA, AWAWA) crossed the open channel without difficulty.
claims.source: As expected given the dimensions of the open channel (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A), all three substrates crossed without difficulty (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on steered MD simulation data shown in Figure 7E.

results.result: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that replacing ADP-BeFx with ATP results in the lateral gate (LG) of SecY either retaining a part-open state (~1.8 nm) or widening to an open state (~2.6 nm), while substitution with ADP causes LG closure to ~1.5 nm in all simulations, closely resembling the resting SecY structure. These conformational changes occur rapidly within the first 10 ns and are consistent across different force fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C35 provide converging computational evidence from MD simulations showing nucleotide-dependent LG conformational changes. The use of multiple independent simulations (C28), validation with different force fields (C32), and comparison with known crystal structures (C31) strengthen the findings. The rapid divergence (C34) and interpretation as a high-energy intermediate (C35) are appropriately qualified.

results.result: MD simulations show that the configuration of helicase motif residues in SecA's nucleotide binding site (NBS) correlates with the open or closed state of the SecY channel, with the NBS being more open in ATP simulations compared to ADP-bound simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C33 and C59 are supported by MD simulation data (Figure 3C and Figure 6A+B). The correlation between NBS configuration and channel state provides mechanistic insight into long-range communication between SecA and SecY, though the pathway of signal transmission is acknowledged as subtle.

results.result: A FRET-based experimental system using doubly-labeled SecY**EG demonstrates that SecA binding causes LG movement, with further FRET decrease upon AMPPNP addition but not ADP. The changes represent differences in LG width rather than binding affinity differences, consistent with MD predictions of nucleotide-dependent channel conformational changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 establish a functional FRET system with appropriate controls (activity assays C37, labeling verification C38, orientation analysis C39) and demonstrate nucleotide-dependent conformational changes. The titration experiments (C42) properly distinguish affinity effects from conformational changes, validating the MD predictions experimentally.

results.result: Single-molecule FRET analysis reveals that SecY**EG exists in three principal conformational states: closed (EFRET ~0.76), part-open (EFRET ~0.59), and open (EFRET ~0.45). AMPPNP favors the open state, ADP favors the closed state, and ATP predominantly populates the part-open state. Mathematical modeling confirms the part-open state is a true intermediate rather than an averaging artifact.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C54, C57 provide rigorous single-molecule evidence with appropriate controls (single FRET pair selection C44), statistical validation (SVD and global fitting C47), and mathematical modeling to exclude artifacts (C53). The identification of three states with nucleotide-dependent populations is well-supported, and the ~0.9 nm distance change (C49) is consistent with MD and crystal structures.

results.result: Addition of pre-protein (pOA) with ATP causes the open state to dominate in single-molecule FRET experiments, consistent with known acceleration of ADP release by pre-protein, without detecting additional channel states.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 demonstrate that pre-protein shifts the equilibrium toward the open state, consistent with established biochemical properties of SecA (C56 citation). The observation that no additional states are detected (C57) is important for model parsimony, though it doesn't exclude transient states below detection limits.

results.result: The combined MD and FRET results establish that nucleotide occupancy in SecA regulates the opening of the SecY protein-channel and lateral gate.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is a well-supported synthesis of the computational (C27-C35) and experimental (C36-C57) findings. The convergence of independent MD simulations and multiple experimental approaches (ensemble and single-molecule FRET) provides strong evidence for nucleotide-dependent channel regulation.

results.result: Two-way communication exists between SecYEG and SecA over >5 nm: trapping the LG in a closed position reduces SecA's affinity for AMPPNP 5-fold and slows ADP release by ~50%, demonstrating that LG conformational state is transmitted to the NBS and controls ATP affinity and ADP release rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 provide experimental evidence for bidirectional communication using a cross-linked LG mutant. The 5-fold reduction in AMPPNP affinity (C61) and 50% reduction in ADP koff (C63) are quantitative measurements supporting the conclusion (C64). However, C60 is speculative and appropriately qualified as inference.

results.result: The increase in ATP turnover caused by LG opening could provide a mechanistic basis for the known allosteric activation of SecA by signal sequence binding into the LG.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 establishes prior knowledge of allosteric activation, but C66 is explicitly speculative ("could provide a basis"). While the hypothesis is reasonable given the demonstrated LG-NBS communication, direct experimental evidence linking signal sequence binding to the observed effects is not provided in this study.

results.result: The two-helix finger (2HF) of SecA, positioned at the SecY channel entrance, acts as a sensor for translocating peptides: cross-linking peptides to the 2HF region increases ADP release rate in a size-dependent manner (bulkier peptides have greater effects), suggesting steric sensing of passing peptides that transmits information back to the NBS.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C75 provide experimental evidence that peptides at the channel entrance affect nucleotide exchange. The position-specific effects (C71 at 2HF but not C at position R20C), size-dependence (C72), and consistency with previous mutation studies (C74, C75) support the conclusion. However, C69 and C75 are appropriately qualified as hypotheses.

results.result: Steered MD simulations demonstrate that the closed SecY channel (ADP-bound state) permits passage of narrow substrates like AGAGA but substantially retards larger substrates like AWAWA, while the open channel (ATP-bound state) allows all tested substrates to pass freely. This indicates the closed conformation selects against bulky stretches, requiring channel opening for their passage.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C85 combine prior knowledge (C76-C79) with new steered MD data (C82-C83) to demonstrate size-selective substrate passage. The experimental design is appropriate, though C81 is speculative. The conclusions (C84-C85) are well-supported by the simulation data and consistent with the overall model.

results.result: The authors propose a Brownian ratchet mechanism for protein translocation where ATP binding by SecA causes long-range opening of the SecY channel, substrates at the channel entrance regulate nucleotide exchange in SecA, and this two-way communication biases the direction of random polypeptide diffusion. The mechanism is directional because energy-dependent blockage resolution occurs only at the cytosolic surface, with irreversible initiation and completion steps ensuring forward movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C104, C123-C125 synthesize the experimental and computational findings into a coherent mechanistic model. The model is well-supported by the demonstrated nucleotide-dependent channel states, bidirectional communication, and substrate sensing. However, the model represents an inference from the data rather than direct observation of the complete translocation cycle.

results.result: The different open and closed states required for the proposed model are represented in various published translocon structures. A recent structure with pseudo pre-protein shows the LG in a part-open state with narrow polypeptide, suggesting the complex might not reach the fully closed state with substrate bound and that further opening would be required for larger substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 appropriately contextualize the findings within existing structural data. The comparison with the recent Li et al. 2016 structure (C106-C109) provides independent validation of the proposed states, though C108-C109 are inferences rather than direct demonstrations.

results.result: The prevailing power-stroke model for SecA-mediated translocation lacks direct evidence, and structural considerations make it unclear how the 2HF could selectively bind and move diverse substrate regions. Immobilization of the 2HF does not prevent translocation, suggesting any power-stroke would need to be extremely subtle.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 provide critical assessment of the existing model based on prior literature (C86, C89) and structural reasoning (C88). This establishes the scientific context and motivation for the alternative Brownian ratchet mechanism, though it represents evaluation of prior work rather than new findings.

results.result: Differential substrate binding between ATP- and ADP-bound SecA states could represent either an additional pre-protein clamp to refine the proposed model or a proof-reading mechanism to prevent substrate jamming, which is known to be deleterious and lead to SecY degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 discuss potential refinements to the model based on prior observations (C110, C113, C114). However, C111 and C112 are explicitly speculative alternatives without experimental discrimination between them in this study. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work rather than established findings.

results.result: The proposed Brownian ratchet model accounts for previously observed properties including translocation intermediates at low ATP, linear dependence of translocation rate on substrate length, and the tight binding of ATP-bound SecA to the channel (which prevents ion leakage from an open channel).
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 demonstrate that the proposed model is consistent with diverse prior observations. C115-C116 show the model explains existing data through inference, while C117 cites prior work and C118 provides functional reasoning. This strengthens the model's plausibility but represents post-hoc explanation rather than prediction.

results.result: The proposed mechanism resembles suggested mechanisms for eukaryotic Sec machinery but with cytosolic ratcheting, may offer a unifying concept for protein transport in other systems (mitochondria, chloroplasts), and parallels two-way communication observed in other molecular motors (helicases, dynein), suggesting a common mechanism for converting chemical energy into directional motion.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122, C126-C127 place the findings in broader context. C119 and C121 cite relevant prior work, but C120, C122, and C127 are explicitly speculative about generalizability. While the parallels are interesting, direct evidence for these broader applications is not provided in this study.

results.result: Background claims establish that the Sec system is the main protein secretion pathway across life, describe the SecYEG/Sec61 translocon structure and function, detail SecA's role as a cytosolic ATPase driving translocation, and note that while ATP turnover is coupled to translocation, the mechanism remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C26 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims set the scientific context but do not represent new findings from this study. C14-C15 and C25 include appropriate speculation about potential functions based on structural features.
